families.s: HSE metalworking-fluid skin, respiratory and fluid-management guidance
families.t: fluid quality, bacterial contamination, mist control, skin protection, enclosure, LEV, surveillance and response to ill health
f: Metalworking fluids are neat oils or water-based fluids used to lubricate and cool metal machining and shaping.
Exposure can cause dermatitis, occupational asthma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, bronchitis and other breathing problems.
Workers may be exposed by inhaling mist, skin contact, broken skin or ingestion through poor hygiene.
COSHH requires exposure by inhalation, ingestion or skin contact to be prevented or adequately controlled.
Fluid quality and bacterial contamination should be monitored and controlled.
Machine enclosures, LEV and other exposure controls must be checked and maintained.
Health surveillance is required where workers are exposed to fluid or mist and should identify early skin or respiratory effects.
Prompt action after suspected ill health should include occupational-health referral, investigation of the cause and review of controls.
families.g: MWF risk depends on formulation, concentration, microbial contamination, machining energy, mist generation, enclosure, ventilation, skin contact, hygiene, fluid maintenance and surveillance.

families.s: HSE occupational health-surveillance scheme and record-keeping guidance
families.t: risk-based repeated checks, worker consultation, scheme design, competent support, action on results, health records and biological monitoring
f: Health surveillance is a scheme of repeated checks used to identify ill health caused by work.
It is legally required where workers remain exposed to specified health risks after controls have been implemented.
A scheme is appropriate where an identifiable effect is linked to exposure, is reasonably likely and can be detected using a valid low-risk technique.
Health-surveillance findings must inform risk assessment and review of exposure controls.
Employers must consult workers and explain the purpose, process, attendance requirements and action following abnormal results.
Schemes should identify exposed groups, competent support, leadership, responsibilities, communications and practical arrangements.
Employers must maintain health records separately from confidential clinical medical records for the required retention period.
Biological monitoring can measure a chemical or metabolite in blood or urine to assess total uptake by all exposure routes.
families.g: Surveillance need and design depend on the hazard, residual exposure, disease relationship, detection method, worker group, frequency, legal regime, competent clinical support and how results change controls.

families.t: flooring, contamination, cleaning, housekeeping, lighting, footwear, maintenance, reporting and worker involvement
f: Employers must assess and control slip-and-trip risks affecting workers and other people.
Workplace floors must be suitable, maintained in good condition and kept free from obstructions.
Simple controls include prompt spill removal, closed drawers, clear routes and suitable storage.
Management systems should plan, train, organise, control, monitor and review cleaning and maintenance arrangements.
Floor design, maintenance, walkway width, stairs, handrails, lighting and distractions affect slip-and-trip risk.
Workers should report hazards and near misses, keep floors clear and dry and use equipment as trained.
Cleaning can create risk through wet smooth floors and trailing cables and therefore requires suitable timing, equipment and segregation.
Slip prevention should address contamination at source, flooring, footwear, cleaning method, housekeeping and human behaviour.
families.g: Slip-and-trip risk depends on floor material and condition, contamination, cleaning method and timing, footwear, lighting, route design, obstructions, weather, behaviour and maintenance response.

families.s: HSE young-worker, work-experience and apprentice protection guidance
families.t: age-related vulnerability, risk assessment, instruction, training, supervision, legal restrictions and cooperation between organisations
f: Employers have the same general health, safety and welfare responsibilities for workers under 18 as for other workers.
Young people are at greater injury risk when new to work because they may lack experience, maturity, physical capability or confidence to raise concerns.
Instruction, training and supervision must be clear, sufficient and proportionate to the actual tasks and risks.
Employers should check that a young person has understood the hazards, controls and instructions.
Young people commonly require closer supervision than experienced adult workers.
A young person is under 18 and a child is below the minimum school-leaving age for the relevant legal restrictions.
Children below minimum school-leaving age are generally prohibited from industrial workplaces except for properly managed work experience.
Employers, apprenticeship agencies, hosts and training providers should cooperate so apprentices receive equivalent protection.
families.g: Young-worker risk depends on age, maturity, physical development, experience, task complexity, induction, supervision, working hours, workplace culture and the effectiveness of host-provider coordination.

families.s: HSE pregnant-worker and new-mother individual risk-assessment guidance
families.t: individual assessment, common hazards, adjustments, alternative work, suspension, night work, rest and breastfeeding facilities
f: Employers must carry out an individual risk assessment for a worker who is pregnant, has given birth within six months or is breastfeeding.
The individual assessment follows written notification and must identify and control risks to the worker and child.
Common risks include prolonged standing or sitting, heavy lifting, unsuitable workstations, hours, stress, temperature and noise.
Where significant risk cannot be controlled, working conditions or hours should first be adjusted.
If adjustment is not possible, suitable alternative work on the same terms should be offered.
If safe alternative work is unavailable, the worker must be suspended on full pay for as long as necessary.
Night work requires suitable day work or paid suspension where the assessment or medical advice identifies risk.
Employers must provide a hygienic private rest area, somewhere to lie down if needed and suitable breastfeeding or milk-storage arrangements.
families.g: Risk depends on pregnancy stage, post-birth recovery, breastfeeding, medical advice, task, posture, hours, substances, infection, noise, vibration, temperature, radiation and available adjustments.

families.s: HSE home and hybrid worker health-and-safety guidance
families.t: proportionate risk assessment, communication, stress, DSE, electrical safety, slips, emergencies, accident reporting and alternative arrangements
f: Employers have the same health and safety responsibilities for home and hybrid workers as for workplace-based workers.
Home-working assessments should consider stress, mental health, computer use and the working environment.
Most home-worker risks can be managed proportionately through discussion, guidance, questionnaires or self-assessment.
Employers should consider work type and duration, communication, safe methods and required controls.
Regular contact, workload review, breaks and access to support help control isolation and stress.
DSE assessments should cover each regular work setting and workers cannot be charged for necessary control measures.
Home workers should receive advice on electrical damage, overloaded extensions, slips, trailing wires and emergency contacts.
A home incident may be reportable under RIDDOR when caused by the work activity or employer-provided equipment.
families.g: Home-working risk depends on task and duration, workstation and environment, isolation, communications, working hours, electrical equipment, other household occupants, emergencies and individual needs.

families.s: HSE shift-work and fatigue risk-management guidance
families.t: assessment, scheduling, sleep loss, night work, alertness, travel, worker differences, monitoring and continuous review
f: Shift work can affect health and safety and should be managed through an assess, act, check and review process.
Employers should assess risks associated with shift patterns rather than relying only on working-time compliance.
Sleep loss and fatigue are major problems for shift workers and daytime sleep is often shorter and poorer quality than night sleep.
Long shifts, night shifts and early starts can increase risk when workers drive to or from work.
Workers vary in their ability to tolerate shift work because of health, age, fitness, lifestyle and domestic responsibilities.
Schedules and personal strategies should support adequate sleep, alertness, rest and safe travel.
Fatigue-risk-management systems should treat hours limits as triggers for further assessment rather than sustainable targets.
Poor control of fatigue and shift work can contribute to major-accident risk as well as individual error and ill health.
families.g: Fatigue risk depends on shift timing, duration and rotation, consecutive duties, workload, breaks, commuting, sleep opportunity and quality, individual factors, overtime and organisational monitoring.

families.s: HSE contractor selection, coordination and site-control guidance
families.t: competence assessment, pre-work information, coordination, supervision, equipment, interfaces, monitoring and subcontractor control
f: Contractors should be selected and assessed as carefully as permanent staff for competence, fitness, qualifications and current certificates.
Contractor activities must fit the overall work scheme without creating unnecessary additional risk.
The site controller must provide contractors with relevant information about the workplace, routes, equipment, hazards and other people.
Contractor and subcontractor suitability should be checked through competence, training, safety standards and previous performance.
Clients should review experience, references, competence certificates, safety performance and health-and-safety management arrangements.
Before work begins, responsibilities, vehicles or equipment, work methods and safety arrangements should be agreed.
Construction contractors must plan, manage and monitor their work and control risks to workers and anyone else affected.
Monitoring and coordination must continue during the work and include interfaces between contractors, site operations and visiting drivers.
families.g: Contractor risk depends on selection, competence evidence, scope clarity, information exchange, supervision, subcontracting, simultaneous activities, site familiarity, equipment, communication and monitoring.
